questions.question: What are the two main sublayers in each transformer encoder block?
options: Multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network
questions.explanation: Each encoder block has: (1) multi-head self-attention, and (2) a position-wise feed-forward network (two linear layers with a ReLU/GELU in between). Both sublayers use residual connections and layer normalization.

questions.question: What is the difference between the encoder and decoder in the original transformer?
options: The encoder processes text, the decoder processes images
The decoder has an additional cross-attention sublayer that attends to encoder outputs
The encoder uses causal masking, the decoder doesn't
They are identical — transformers only use encoders
questions.explanation: The decoder has three sublayers: (1) masked self-attention (causal), (2) cross-attention over encoder outputs, (3) feed-forward. The cross-attention allows the decoder to 'read' the encoded source while generating the target sequence.

questions.question: Why does the transformer decoder use causal (masked) self-attention?
options: To prevent the decoder from attending to future tokens when generating each output token
questions.explanation: During training, the full target sequence is provided, but generation is auto-regressive — each token should only see previous tokens, not future ones. Causal masking sets future attention scores to -∞ before softmax, zeroing their weights.

questions.question: What does Pre-LN (Pre-Layer Norm) vs Post-LN refer to in transformer architecture?
options: Whether layer norm is applied before or after the residual connection
Whether layer norm is applied before or after the attention sublayer's input
Whether layer norm replaces batch norm
Whether to use RMS norm or layer norm
questions.explanation: Post-LN (original paper): LN after residual add. Pre-LN (modern LLMs like GPT-2+): LN before the sublayer, inside the residual branch. Pre-LN gives more stable training at scale and is the de facto standard in modern architectures.

questions.question: What is the typical ratio of the FFN hidden dimension to d_model?
questions.explanation: The original paper used d_ff = 4 × d_model. This ratio has remained standard — e.g., d_model=4096, d_ff=16384 in LLaMA. The FFN's large hidden layer stores factual knowledge and acts as key-value memory.
